rv.q: He wears his learning on his sleeve but beneath that beats a heart and electrifying artistic purpose.
And yet, somehow, Stoppard, Russell Beale and Tennyson find a light in Housman you might never have imagined.
The quicksilver Russell Beale is a vocal glory, leaping in a breath from flute to poignant bassoon, from wit to sorrow.
Not to mention the fact you’ll feel about a thousand times cleverer after seeing it.
McIntyre funnels a stream of fine performances, with many actors multi-roling, into a play that, for the most part, sweeps the audience away.
Beale portrays everything from suppressed desolation to waspish put-downs with his customary deftness.
This first London revival of that much-admired 1997 play offers plenty of pleasures, not least a characteristically lucid and tender central turn from Simon Russell Beale.
Performed with levity and tenderness as it is, at three hours it's beyond most people's endurance.
It’s worth watching, but it’s somewhat sloggy, and I wonder if for once a more conventional playwright might have articulated this all in a more gripping, incisive fashion.

My advice is to look beyond the wordplay to something more wondrous – a play that feels, misleadingly, like homework yet comes possessed to those willing to open themselves to it of a lasting capacity to crack open the heart.
It’s in this tone that the play continues, keeping an otherwise potentially alienated audience enthralled by its carefully timed, easy wit.
On the whole it was a terrific effort.

Simon Russell Beale as the elder Housman and Matthew Tennyson as the younger movingly reveal a central character who finds consolation in poetry and scholarship but remains haunted by an enduring love, one he can neither express nor attain.
You will struggle to get a ticket to this excellent revival; but you will also struggle to find a more rewarding theatrical night out among current offerings.
This is an evening which has many joys and pleasures, although its masculine verbosity will not be to everyone’s taste.
All in all, I really wanted to love The Invention of Love , but in the end it left me a bit cold.

cn.t: Stoppard's dense 1997 meditation on A.E. Housman gets a mostly lauded Hampstead revival, with Simon Russell Beale universally praised. Critics split on accessibility—brilliant but demanding, rewarding the tenacious while potentially exhausting casual theatergoers.
